name: bib-fetch
description: Fetch official, correct BibTeX for a list of citations and return each entry re-keyed to the user's exact citation key; also verify/audit existing .bib entries against authoritative sources (DBLP, publisher DOI record, Crossref, arXiv). Trigger on prompts like "Fetch OFFICIAL BibTeX for the citations below and return each RE-KEYED to the given cite key. READ-ONLY", "find the official bibtex", "verify bibliography entries", "check my .bib", "are these references correct", "You are researching bibliography entries for an academic paper survey", or any pasted list of cite keys plus titles/authors where the user expects BibTeX back. Do NOT trigger for literature discovery or survey research (deciding WHICH papers to cite), writing related-work prose, fixing \cite or \bibliographystyle usage in .tex files, or citation-style questions that involve no source lookup.
---

# bib-fetch: official BibTeX retrieval and .bib verification

Fetch authoritative BibTeX for requested citations, re-key each entry to the
user's key, and report every field you could not confirm. Accuracy over
completeness: a missing field is a nuisance; an invented one is a retraction
risk and referees do check.

## Scope fence

Treat the task as READ-ONLY unless the user explicitly asks you to update a
.bib file. Bibliography files are shared across papers and version-controlled;
an unrequested edit contaminates diffs the user will later have to explain.
Deliver a paste-ready block instead. If a project CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md
prescribes bibliography conventions (key scheme, venue abbreviation style,
file layout), those win over anything below.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the request.** Build a list of (user-key, citation hint) pairs. If
   verifying an existing .bib, read it first and note the venue-abbreviation
   style already in use (e.g. "Proc. IEEE S&P" vs. full proceedings titles) so
   new entries match — an inconsistent .bib looks careless in a submission.
2. **Look up each entry from authoritative sources.** Work entries in
   parallel with subagents if available; otherwise iterate. Useful endpoints
   (all reachable with plain `curl` or a web-fetch capability):
   - DBLP search: `https://dblp.org/search/publ/api?q=<title>&format=json`,
     then fetch clean BibTeX from `https://dblp.org/rec/<dblp-key>.bib`
   - DOI content negotiation: `curl -sL -H "Accept: application/x-bibtex" https://doi.org/<doi>`
   - Crossref: `https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=<title>&rows=3`
   - arXiv export API: `https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?id_list=<id>`
3. **Prefer the published record over arXiv.** When a peer-reviewed version
   exists, cite it (publisher/DBLP record), not the preprint: referees notice
   arXiv-only citations of published work and read them as sloppiness. Use
   the arXiv record only when no published version exists, and then include
   `eprint`, `archivePrefix={arXiv}`, and `primaryClass` so the entry is
   unambiguous.
4. **Cross-check fields against at least one independent source.** Publisher
   BibTeX exporters add noise (stray `month`, `numpages`, HTML entities) and
   Crossref sometimes mangles diacritics, so reconcile:
   - authors: full list, no silent truncation, spelling and diacritics
     exactly as the authors write them (check DBLP or the paper PDF)
   - year, venue string, volume/number, pages, DOI
   - entry type: conference vs. journal version of the same paper is the
     single most common bibliography error — confirm which one is intended
   - title casing: brace-protect acronyms and proper nouns ({BB84}, {QKD},
     {Coq}, {IEEE}) so bibliography styles cannot lowercase them — publisher
     exports often ship titles unprotected
5. **Flag claim/reference mismatches.** If the user's paper text (or the hint
   they gave) says something the official record contradicts — wrong year,
   "journal version" that is actually a workshop paper, misattributed
   authors — report it explicitly. This is often what the user is really
   hunting for.
6. **Never invent a field.** If pages, DOI, or any field cannot be confirmed
   from a source, omit it and list it under "Unconfirmed fields" with the
   reason. Do not copy a field from a lookalike entry.
7. **Preserve the user's keys exactly** — byte-for-byte, including case.
   The keys are load-bearing: the user's .tex already cites them, and a
   "corrected" key silently breaks the build.

If a hint is ambiguous (two plausible papers match), present both candidates
with sources and ask; never pick one silently.

## Output format

Emit exactly this structure so results are paste-ready and auditable:

```
## BibTeX (paste-ready)

@inproceedings{<user-key>,
  author    = {...},
  title     = {...},
  ...
}

(one block per requested key, in the order requested)

## Discrepancy report

| Key | Field | Claimed / expected | Found (official) | Source URL |
|-----|-------|--------------------|------------------|------------|
| ... | year  | 1984 (paper text)  | 2014 (TCS reprint) | https://doi.org/... |

(write "none" if empty)

## Unconfirmed fields

- <key>: <field> — not present in DBLP or the publisher record; omitted.

(write "none" if empty)
```

## Worked examples

**Re-key + version flag.** Request: `bb84 — Bennett & Brassard, quantum
cryptography public key distribution`. DBLP holds two records: the 1984
IEEE conference paper and the 2014 Theoretical Computer Science reprint
(which carries the DOI). Return the entry re-keyed to `bb84`, pick the
version consistent with what the user's text claims (a sentence citing "the
1984 protocol" wants the 1984 record), and put the other version in the
discrepancy report so the user can choose deliberately.

**arXiv-only entry.** Request: `smith2024lattice — Smith et al., lattice
attacks on X`. DBLP and Crossref show no published version, so return:

```
@misc{smith2024lattice,
  author        = {Smith, Jane and Doe, Richard},
  title         = {Lattice Attacks on X},
  year          = {2024},
  eprint        = {2403.01234},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  primaryClass  = {quant-ph}
}
```

and note under Unconfirmed fields: "smith2024lattice: no peer-reviewed
version found on DBLP/Crossref as of <date>; arXiv record used."

Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.

\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
such that the following
  holds.
  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
  \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
			 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
    \end{split}
  \end{equation*}
  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
	whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.

Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
\end{enumerate}

As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.

To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
\end{proof}






\subsubsection{Complexity of the classical low-degree test.}
The CL functions and decision procedure of the low-degree test are incorporated
as subroutines in some of the normal form verifiers constructed in subsequent
sections.
The next lemma establishes the time complexity of these procedures as a function
of the parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$.
The lemma also establishes the time complexity of computing the {description} of
the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ as a Turing machine, given the parameter
tuple $\ldparams$ as input.

\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}]
	\label{thm:linearity}
	\uses{def:povm-distance}
	Let $0 \le \delta \le 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let

	set of observables indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ acting on
	$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}$, and suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen
	uniformly at random from $\F_2^t$ the approximate linearity
	\[
		(\mathcal{O}^u \, \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\mathsf{A}}
		\approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\mathsf{A}}
	\]

	$\ket{\psi'}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{B}}
	= \ket{\psi}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}} \ot \ket{0}_{\mathsf{A}'}$
	in an extended space
	$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{B}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{A}'}$ and
	observables $\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ acting on
	$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{A}'}$ with the following two

	\label{rem:linearity-import}

	first step is an unresolved obligation of the source argument, recorded

	\cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}; the construction below is
	carried out for the parameters for which the distribution is defined.

	\emph{fresh diagonal direction pair} we mean a pair $(s', w')$ with
	$s'$ uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $w' \in \F_q^m$ having coordinates
	$1, \dots, \chi(s')-1$ equal to $0$ and the remaining coordinates
	uniformly random; this is exactly the law of the coordinate--direction
	data of the diagonal component of the line-point distribution over
	$\F_q^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:line-point-dist}).

	If $\ell$ is axis-parallel, $\ell = (v, e_j)$ with
	$v = (v_X, v_Z, \alpha_0, \beta_0)$ and $j \in \{1, \dots, 2m+2\}$, set
	$\ell_X = (v'_X, e_{i_X})$ and $\ell_Z = (v'_Z, e_{i_Z})$ where: for
	$1 \le j \le m$, $i_X = j$ and $i_Z$ is uniformly random in
	$\{1,\dots,m\}$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$, $i_X$ is uniformly random and
	$i_Z = j - m$; for $2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both $i_X$ and $i_Z$ are
	uniformly random; and $v'_X, v'_Z$ are the canonical line
	representatives of $v_X, v_Z$ for the chosen directions
	(Definition~\ref{def:line-representative}), so that $v_X \in \ell_X$
	and $v_Z \in \ell_Z$.

	the diagonal component of the line-point distribution
	(Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} instantiated at
	dimension $2m+2$) the direction $w = (w_X, w_Z, \gamma, \delta)$ has
	coordinates $1, \dots, j-1$ equal to $0$, where $j = \chi_{2m+2}(s)$,
	and its remaining coordinates are uniformly random. These remaining

	at index $j$ and may be the zero vector, in which case $\ell$ is a
	singleton (Definition~\ref{def:line}).

	% nonzero coordinate is j = chi(s)"

	uniformly random in the class $\chi^{-1}(j)$ and $s_Z$ uniformly
	random in the class $\chi^{-1}(1)$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$, the pair
	$(s_X, w'_X)$ is a fresh diagonal direction pair and $w'_Z = w_Z$,
	with $s_Z$ uniformly random in the class $\chi^{-1}(j-m)$; for
	$2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both $(s_X, w'_X)$ and $(s_Z, w'_Z)$ are fresh
	diagonal direction pairs, sampled independently; and $v'_X, v'_Z$ are
	the canonical representatives of $v_X, v_Z$ for the directions
	$w'_X, w'_Z$.

	axis-parallel, both $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ are constructed to be
	axis-parallel. The containments in Property~2 hold for every point
	$u^\dagger = (u^\dagger_X, u^\dagger_Z, \alpha^\dagger,
	\beta^\dagger)$ of $\ell$: the block $u^\dagger_X$ differs from $v_X$
	by a multiple of the direction of $\ell_X$ when that direction is
	inherited from $\ell$ (namely $e_j$ for axis-parallel $\ell$ with
	$1 \le j \le m$, and $w_X$ for diagonal $\ell$ with $1 \le j \le m$),
	and equals $v_X$ in all other cases, since then the corresponding
	block of the direction of $\ell$ vanishes; in either case
	$u^\dagger_X \in \ell_X$ because $v_X \in \ell_X$, and symmetrically
	$u^\dagger_Z \in \ell_Z$.

	$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is a function of $\ell$ and of the auxiliary
	randomness alone: the directions used are either read off from the
	direction data of $\ell$ or freshly sampled, and by
	Proposition~\ref{prop:line-equiv} the canonical representatives
	$v'_X, v'_Z$ do not depend on which base point of $\ell$ is used to
	compute them. Under both components of the line-point distribution the
	point $u$ is uniformly distributed on $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and, conditioned
	on the line $\ell$, uniformly distributed on the points of $\ell$
	(each of the $q$ values of the line parameter, or the single point
	when the direction vanishes, being equally likely). Hence, conditioned
	on $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$, the sampled point $u$ is uniformly
	distributed on $\ell$, and it suffices to establish the claimed
	mixture description for the tuple $(\ell_X, \ell_Z, u)$ produced by
	the procedure itself.

	Condition on the component of the line-point distribution
	(axis-parallel or diagonal) and on $j$; the mixture of Property~2 is
	over these choices together with the fresh index choices, and the
	blocks $u_X, u_Z$ of $u$ are independent and uniform on $\F_q^m$,
	independent of all direction data. In the axis-parallel case with
	$1 \le j \le m$, the pair $(\ell_X, u_X)$ consists of the uniformly
	random point $u_X$ together with the canonical axis-parallel line
	through it in direction $e_j$, so
	$(\ell_X, u_X) \sim D_{\mathrm{ALine},j}$, while, conditioned
	additionally on $i_Z$, the pair $(\ell_Z, u_Z)$ consists of the
	uniformly random point $u_Z$ together with the canonical line through
	it in direction $e_{i_Z}$, so
	$(\ell_Z, u_Z) \sim D_{\mathrm{ALine},i_Z}$; the two pairs are
	functions of the disjoint independent data $u_X$ and $(u_Z, i_Z)$,
	hence independent. In the diagonal case with $1 \le j \le m$, the
	triple $(u_X, w_X, s_X)$ has $u_X$ uniform, $w_X$ with coordinates
	$1, \dots, j-1$ equal to $0$ and the remaining coordinates uniform,
	and $s_X$ uniform in $\chi^{-1}(j)$, which is exactly the law
	generating $D_{\mathrm{DLine},j}$; hence
	$(\ell_X, u_X) \sim D_{\mathrm{DLine},j}$, and similarly
	$(\ell_Z, u_Z) \sim D_{\mathrm{DLine},1}$ since $w_Z$ is uniform and
	$s_Z$ is uniform in $\chi^{-1}(1)$; the two pairs are functions of the
	disjoint independent data $(u_X, w_X, s_X)$ and $(u_Z, w_Z, s_Z)$,
	hence independent. The remaining cases are analogous: each of
	$(\ell_X, u_X)$ and $(\ell_Z, u_Z)$ is either built from the inherited
	direction block as above, or from a fresh axis index or fresh diagonal
	direction pair, in which case it is distributed as the uniform mixture
	over $i$ of $D_{\mathrm{v},i}$ for the corresponding type
	$\mathrm{v}$; and the two pairs are always functions of disjoint
	independent collections of the variables $u_X$, $u_Z$, the direction
	blocks, and the fresh auxiliary choices, hence independent conditioned
	on the component. Within each component this yields exactly the
	description of Property~2: the pair $(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is
	product-distributed according to the line marginals of
	$D_{\mathrm{v},i}$ and $D_{\mathrm{v},j}$, and, conditioned on
	$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, each of $u_X$ and $u_Z$ is uniformly distributed
	on its line, because under each restricted distribution the point is
	uniform on the line conditionally on the line. The equivalent product
	formulations follow from the same conditional uniformity.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Commuting and anticommuting tuples]
	\label{def:anticommuting-tuple}
	% The quantity gamma is introduced in the source at eq:gamma-value, inside
	% the completeness analysis of the Pauli basis test; that label has no
	% corresponding node here, so the definition below is self-contained.
	\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:subfield-trace}
	For a tuple
	$\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z) \in (\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$, let
	\[
		\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\big( (r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)) \cdot (r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)) \big)\,,
	\]
	where $r_W \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_W)$ is the scalar multiple of the
	vector $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_W) \in \F_q^{M}$, the middle $\cdot$ is the
	$\F_q$-inner product of two vectors in $\F_q^{M}$, and
	$\tr = \tr_{q \to 2}$. The tuple $\omega$ is called \emph{anticommuting}
	if $\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma(\omega) = 0$.
\end{definition}

The sign $(-1)^{\gamma(\omega)}$ is exactly the sign with which the
generalized Pauli observables $\tau^X(r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X))$ and
$\tau^Z(r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z))$ commute
(see Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation});
this is the source of the terminology.

\begin{lemma}[Probability of anticommuting tuples]
	\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
	% The source states this result in a `fact' environment; fact environments
	% become lemma nodes and the paper label is kept verbatim.
	% The exact value of the anticommuting probability and the constant lower
	% bounds under the hypothesis m <= q are additions relative to the source,
	% which asserts only the two bounds displayed at the end of the statement;
	% the source states those bounds without the hypothesis m, d >= 1, under
	% which alone they hold (see the remark following this lemma). The
	% unconditional constant bounds are what the proof of the lemma labelled
	% lem:qld-win-implications uses.
	\uses{def:anticommuting-tuple}
	A tuple $\omega = (u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)$ sampled uniformly at random from
	$(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$ is anticommuting with probability exactly
	\[
		\big(1 - q^{-1}\big)^{m+1} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\,,
	\]
	and commuting with the complementary probability, which is at least
	$\frac12$. In particular, if $m \leq q$, then $\omega$ is anticommuting
	with probability at least $2^{-4}$ and commuting with probability at
	least $\frac12$. If $m, d \geq 1$, then the probability that $\omega$ is
	anticommuting is at least
	\[
		(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big(1 - \frac{md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}
		\,\geq\, \Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}\,,
	\]
	and the probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least
	$\big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
	\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:indicator-vector, def:admissible-size, def:binary-representation, lem:downsize_field, lem:one}
	By the definition of the indicator vector
	(Definition~\ref{def:indicator-vector}), expanding the product over the
	coordinates $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ into a sum over $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
	gives
	\[
		\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)
		\,=\, \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(u_X)\, \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(u_Z)
		\,=\, \prod_{i=1}^{m} \big( u_{X,i}\, u_{Z,i} + (1 - u_{X,i})(1 - u_{Z,i}) \big)\,,
	\]
	and since $\F_q$ has characteristic $2$, the $i$-th factor equals
	$1 + u_{X,i} + u_{Z,i}$. Hence
	\[
		\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\Big( (r_X r_Z) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^{m} (1 + u_{X,i} + u_{Z,i}) \Big)\,.
	\]
	For any fixed $u_X$, the $m$ factors $1 + u_{X,i} + u_{Z,i}$ are
	independent and uniformly distributed in $\F_q$ over the choice of
	$u_Z$, so all of them are nonzero with probability $(1-q^{-1})^m$;
	independently, $r_X \neq 0$ with probability $1 - q^{-1}$. If $r_X = 0$
	or some factor vanishes, then $\gamma(\omega) = 0$. Otherwise, over the
	uniform choice of $r_Z$, the argument of the trace is a uniformly random
	element of $\F_q$. Since $q = 2^k$ is admissible, the trace of an
	element of $\F_q$ equals the coordinate sum of its binary
	representation: writing $\kappa$ for the binary representation with
	respect to the fixed self-dual normal basis
	(Definition~\ref{def:binary-representation}), item~2 of
	Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
	$\tr(c) = \tr(c \cdot 1) = \kappa(c) \cdot \kappa(1)$, and $\kappa(1)$
	is the all-ones vector by Lemma~\ref{lem:one}. As $\kappa$ is a
	bijection onto $\F_2^k$, a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ has trace
	$0$ with probability exactly $\frac12$. Combining, the probability that
	$\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$ is exactly $(1-q^{-1})^{m+1} \cdot \frac12$, and
	the probability that $\omega$ is commuting is the complement, which is
	at least $\frac12$.

	If $m \leq q$, then
	$(1-q^{-1})^{m+1} \geq (1-q^{-1})^{q+1} = (1-q^{-1})^{q} \cdot (1-q^{-1})$,
	a product of two positive functions of $q$ that are nondecreasing for
	$q \geq 2$, so it is minimized at $q = 2$, where it equals $2^{-3}$;
	hence the anticommuting probability is at least $2^{-4}$.

	Finally, suppose $m, d \geq 1$, and consider the first inequality of
	the display, which bounds the anticommuting probability from below.
	If $md > q$, that lower bound is negative --- it is the product of
	the positive factors $1 - q^{-m}$, $1 - q^{-1}$, and $\frac12$ with
	the negative factor $1 - md/q$ --- so the anticommuting probability,
	being nonnegative, exceeds it. If $md \leq q$, then by Bernoulli's
	inequality

	where the last step multiplies the nonnegative quantity $1 - md/q$

	anticommuting probability is at least the first displayed bound. For
	the second inequality of the display, expanding the product shows
	that $(1-q^{-m})(1-q^{-1})(1-md/q)$ exceeds

	The commuting probability is at least

Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game
  and let $\strategy = (\psi, A, B)$, $\strategy' = (\psi', A', B')$ be 
  strategies for $\game$.
  For $\delta\in[0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\strategy$ is $\delta$-close to
    $\strategy'$} if the following conditions hold.
  \begin{enumerate}
	\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same
    Hilbert space $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
	\item For all $x \in \cal{X}, y \in \cal{Y}$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta
    (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations
    holding under the distribution $\mu$, and on either $\ket{\psi}$ or
    $\ket{\psi'}$.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

We record several useful facts about the consistency measure and the
state-dependent distance without proof.
Readers are referred to Sections 4.4 and 4.5 in~\cite{NW19} for additional
discussion and proofs.

\begin{fact}[Fact 4.13 and Fact 4.14 in~\cite{NW19}]
  \label{fact:agreement}
  For POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$, the following hold.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item If $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$ then
    $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$.
    \label{item:consistency-implies-approx}
  \item If $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$

name: faithfulness-audit
description: Audit whether a Coq/Rocq or Lean formalization is faithful to its mathematical source (paper/thesis TeX, often under a context/ directory). Compares each formal lemma/definition to the TeX statement it claims to formalize — quantifiers, constants, exponents, side conditions, hidden hypotheses, proof route — and traces axiom/Admitted/sorry provenance, classifying every gap as paper-level abstraction vs cheating assumption. Do NOT use for writing or completing proofs (removing Admitted by proving goals — use coq), whole-manuscript pre-submission scrutiny where the paper's claims, numbers, and novelty are the audit target (use paper-scrutiny), bare admit/sorry counting or closed-vs-tainted status dashboards with no TeX comparison (use proof-status), general code review or refactoring, LaTeX editing or paper writing, software security audits, or dependency/license audits.

# Faithfulness Audit

Verify that a formal development (Coq/Rocq, Lean, or similar) proves what its
mathematical source states — no more, no less — and that nothing unproven
props it up. The failure mode this guards against is subtle: a development
that compiles, shows zero `Admitted`, and still certifies the wrong theorem
because a quantifier moved, a constant halved, or a hypothesis quietly
assumed the hard part.

## Ground rules

- **Read-only.** Do not edit proof files, TeX, or mapping files during the
  audit. An audit that fixes as it goes destroys its own evidence and tempts
  you to patch a symptom (the constant) before the cause (a hypothesis
  mismatch) is characterized. If the prompt asks to *fix* faithfulness, run
  the full audit on the item first, present the report, then edit only what
  the report flags.
- **Project docs win.** Read the project's CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / README
  first. If they prescribe a mapping file, an accepted-axiom whitelist, a
  verdict vocabulary, or a route-fidelity requirement, those override the
  defaults below.
- **Compilation is not faithfulness.** Never report "faithful" from a green
  build; every verdict needs statement-level evidence you quote in the report.

## Procedure

### 1. Locate the audit index
Look for a mapping file (e.g. `ownership.md`) that maps formal source files
to TeX sections; if present it defines the item list and the anchors — use it
as-is. Otherwise build the index yourself: enumerate theorem/lemma/definition
names in the formal sources, grep the TeX for `\begin{theorem}`, `\label`,
equation tags, and pair them by name, comment, or content. List anything you
cannot pair under "Unmapped" — unmapped items are findings, not noise.

### 2. Run five checks per item
1. **Statement match.** Put the TeX statement and the formal statement side
   by side. Compare quantifier order and scope, constants and exponents,
   inequality direction and strictness, side conditions (`n >= 1`, `eps > 0`,
   normalization), and implicit conventions (log base, probability space,
   adversary model). These are exactly the places a formalization drifts
   while staying well-typed and provable, so check them term by term.
2. **Proof-route match, where the project demands it.** If the project claims
   to formalize *the paper's proof* (check the docs and paper text for that
   claim), confirm the formal proof follows the paper's decomposition — same
   key lemmas, same argument — not an alternative shortcut. A shortcut can
   prove a superficially identical statement whose meaning has shifted (e.g.
   a weaker adversary model makes the bound trivial), and it forfeits the
   claim that the paper's argument is machine-checked. If the docs make no
   route claim, note route divergence as an observation, not a failure.
3. **No silent strengthening or weakening.** Diff hypotheses and conclusion
   against the TeX. Added hypotheses strengthen what is assumed; relaxed
   bounds or dropped conjuncts weaken what is delivered. Both hide inside
   project-local definitions the TeX does not share — unfold them.
4. **Gap classification.** For every gap, decide which it is. A *paper-level
   abstraction* works at the same level the paper does (classical reals,
   finite dimensions when the paper is finite-dimensional, standard-library
   classical axioms the project whitelists) and may stand. A *cheating
   assumption* assumes something the paper proves, or something stronger than
   the paper assumes, and must be discharged before the result can be
   claimed. The distinction is what the whole audit turns on — when unsure,
   ask what the paper's referee would say if shown the assumption.
5. **Hypothesis provenance.** Before compiling anything for the closure
   check, look for a running build (`pgrep -fl 'coqc|dune|lake|make'`) and
   reuse fresh compiled artifacts; keep at most 2 live prover processes.
   Compute the assumption closure of each top-level theorem — `Print
   Assumptions <thm>.` in Coq/Rocq, `#print axioms <thm>` in Lean — and grep
   the dependency files for
   `Admitted|admit|Axiom|Parameter|Hypothesis|sorry`. Nuance:
   `Hypothesis`/`Variable` inside a Section are discharged into the
   statement (premises, not taint), and `Parameter`/`Axiom` inside a
   `Module Type` is an interface declaration — classify these separately;
   only declarations that appear in the Print Assumptions closure are
   candidate taint. Taint propagates: one upstream `Admitted` makes every
   downstream theorem conditional, however clean its own proof looks. Quote
   the tool output verbatim.

### 3. Scale to the item count
For large indices, spawn parallel subagents if available (one per TeX section
or source file) and merge their tables; otherwise iterate sequentially. In
either case run the provenance commands in a shell yourself, so verdicts rest
on tool output rather than on reading the sources.

## Verdicts
- **faithful** — statement matches (and route, where required); assumption
  closure is empty or whitelisted by project docs.
- **divergent** — statement differs materially from the TeX, or the route
  diverges where the project demands route fidelity.
- **cheat** — depends on an undischarged cheating assumption.
- **unproven** — the item or something in its closure is `Admitted`/`sorry`.

An item receives the worst verdict among its findings.

## Output format

```
## Faithfulness audit — <formal target> vs <TeX source>
Index: <mapping file used, or "built ad hoc">   Scope: <files / sections>

| Formal name (file:line) | Source anchor | Verdict | Evidence | Required action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fail_bound (security.v:88) | Thm 4.2, Eq. (4.7) | divergent | TeX exponent -n*eps^2/2; formal -n*eps^2 | match exponent or cite where the sharper bound is proved |

### Assumption closure
<theorem>: <verbatim Print Assumptions / #print axioms output>, each entry
classified abstraction / cheat / whitelisted.

### Unmapped
Formal items with no TeX anchor; TeX claims with no formal counterpart.

### Summary
N faithful / N divergent / N cheat / N unproven.
One-line judgment: does the development support the stated goal, e.g.
"faithful and full formal verification of <claim> as defined in <source>"?
```

## Worked examples

**Divergent constant.** TeX Eq. (4.7) bounds failure by `2*exp(-n*eps^2/2)`;
the formal lemma states `<= 2*exp(-n*eps^2)`. Verdict: divergent — do not
wave it through as "the formal bound is stronger". A sharper claim than the
paper proves is still divergent: either the proof cheats upstream, it proves
a different theorem, or the formalization legitimately tightened the bound
and the TeX must be updated to match — reconcile whichever side is wrong
before claiming correspondence.

**Cheat vs abstraction.** `Hypothesis attack_iid : eve = iid_channel e.`
while the TeX proves security against coherent attacks — verdict: cheat. It
assumes away the paper's hardest step (the reduction from coherent to
collective attacks); required action is to discharge it via the paper's own
argument or re-scope the claim. Contrast `Classical_Prop.classic` appearing
in the closure of a classically-argued paper — abstraction; record it and
suggest whitelisting in the project docs if not already there.

## Closing the audit
End with the report — no edits, no "quick fixes" on the way out. If the user
asked for a fix, the required-action column is the work order: confirm it
with the user (or proceed if the prompt already authorized fixing), and only
then leave read-only mode.

# LaTeX editing conventions

Apply these rules to every edit of a `.tex` file.
If the project's CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md prescribes different conventions, the project docs win — this skill fills the gaps they leave.
Venue rules (double-blind anonymity, page budget, formatting requirements of e.g. an IEEE S&P submission) likewise override anything below: never add author-identifying text to an anonymized draft, and treat the page budget as a hard constraint.

## Semantic line breaks

Put one sentence per source line; break long sentences at clause boundaries (after commas, semicolons, or before `\cite`/`\ref`-heavy tails).
Why: version control diffs then show exactly which sentence changed. A reflowed paragraph turns a one-word fix into a 15-line diff that no coauthor can review.

- When editing one sentence, never rewrap the surrounding paragraph.
- When asked to *reformat* to semantic line breaks, change line breaks only: the text must be word-for-word identical after joining lines. Verify with a whitespace-insensitive diff (e.g. `git diff --word-diff` showing no changes).

## Tighten-by-N% protocol

When asked to tighten or compress prose by roughly N%:

1. Edit only the named file or section — scope fences are literal, not suggestions.
2. Compress by cutting filler ("it is worth noting that"), merging redundant sentences, and turning nominalizations into verbs — never by dropping information.
3. Treat these as invariants that must survive byte-for-byte or meaning-for-meaning:
   - every number, unit, and tolerance;
   - all math, inline and display;
   - every `\cite`, `\ref`, `\eqref`, `\label` key;
   - theorem/lemma/definition statements (mathematical content verbatim);
   - defined terms and notation introduced elsewhere in the paper;
   - the tense of claims ("we prove" vs. "we will prove") and the hedging level ("suggests" is not "shows").
4. Land within a couple of points of the target. If N% is unreachable without breaking an invariant, stop short and say which invariant blocked you — undershooting is acceptable, changing a fact is not.

Why the hedging rule gets its own line: compression edits silently upgrade claims ("our results suggest" → "we establish") more often than they change numbers, and for a paper backed by machine-checked proofs the exact strength of each claim is part of the technical content.

## Wording-only safety check

After any copy-edit (yours or one you are reviewing for prose damage), diff old against new and verify zero changes to numbers, math, citation/reference/label keys, theorem statements, and defined terms.
Make the key check mechanical rather than by eye, e.g.:

```sh
mkdir -p tmp   # scratch files go in tmp/, never into the paper source tree
grep -oE '\\[A-Za-z]*(cite|ref|label)[A-Za-z]*\*?\{[^}]*\}' old.tex | sort > tmp/keys.old
grep -oE '\\[A-Za-z]*(cite|ref|label)[A-Za-z]*\*?\{[^}]*\}' new.tex | sort > tmp/keys.new
diff tmp/keys.old tmp/keys.new   # must be empty
```

This pattern also catches natbib/cleveref/hyperref variants (`\citep`, `\citet`, `\cref`, `\Cref`, `\autoref`, `\pageref`, starred forms), but optional-argument forms (`\citep[p.~3]{key}`) escape any brace-anchored pattern — finish with a `git diff --word-diff` scan for cite/ref tokens.

Why: an edit that improves flow but flips a constant or drops a citation is worse than no edit, and the checklist turns the author's re-review from re-reading into spot-checking.

## Stability and restraint

- Keep `\label` names and bib keys stable across edits. Other files, coauthors' in-flight branches, and reviewer responses reference them; renaming a label is a repo-wide change, not a copy-edit.
- Introduce no new macros or packages and do not restructure sections unless explicitly asked. Macro vocabulary and section architecture are paper-level decisions the authors own.
- Match the paper's existing voice. Reuse its established terminology; when choosing between a punchy adjective and the standard term of art, pick the term of art. This author keeps precise words like "intrinsically" but rejects constructions like "a tight parameter accounting argument" as sounding unprofessional — marketing adjectives ("novel", "powerful", "tight" as praise) read as filler in a proofs paper.

## Output format for copy-edit tasks

```
## Edited text
(the edited passage, or a pointer to the applied diff)

## Compression report
- Words before: 412
- Words after: 356
- Change: -13.6% (target: ~12-15%)
(count with the same method before and after, e.g. `detex file.tex | wc -w`)

## Facts preserved
- [x] Numbers/units: unchanged
- [x] Math: unchanged
- [x] \cite keys: 9/9 identical (mechanical diff)
- [x] \ref/\label keys: 14/14 identical (mechanical diff)
- [x] Theorem/lemma statements: verbatim
- [x] Defined terms: unchanged
- [x] Claim tense and hedging: unchanged
```

Any box you cannot tick honestly means the edit is not wording-only: either revert that change or flag it explicitly as a factual change needing author sign-off.

For long files, split the diff-and-verify work per section — spawn parallel subagents if available, otherwise iterate section by section.

## Worked example

Original:
```
It is worth noting that the key rate that is achieved by our protocol is
intrinsically robust to detector noise, as suggested by the results in
Section~\ref{sec:eval}.
```

Good tighten (-38% here; keeps the author's "intrinsically", the hedge "suggested", and the `\ref` key):
```
The key rate is intrinsically robust to detector noise,
as suggested in Section~\ref{sec:eval}.
```

Bad tighten (same length savings, but upgrades the hedge — a factual change):
```
The key rate is provably robust to detector noise (Section~\ref{sec:eval}).
```

   261	conclusion is vacuous: $md \ge q/2$ gives
   262	$\delta_S \ge a(md)^a q^{-b} \ge a\,2^{-a} q^{a-b} \ge a\,2^{-b} \ge 1$
   263	for $a \ge 2$, while the consistency quantities bounded by the theorem never
   264	exceed $1$.  This route stays inside the present definitions but reworks the
   265	sub-line distribution (a fourth coordinate block of dummies), the combining
   266	map, and the wrong-block Schwartz--Zippel analysis, and it moves the
   267	combining lemmas away from their source statements at dimension $2m+2$.
   268	
   269	\paragraph{Unequal index classes.}
   270	One could instead define an index function at dimension $2m+2$ with classes
   271	of sizes $\lfloor q/(2m+2)\rfloor$ and $\lceil q/(2m+2)\rceil$.  The index
   272	is then only approximately uniform, the identification with the external
   273	test fails exactly, and every distributional identity in the sub-line
   274	analysis acquires an error term; this amounts to re-proving the imported
   275	soundness theorem for a perturbed game and is not recommended.
   276	
   277	\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
   278	
   279	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} keeps the sub-line lemma, the
   280	combined line lemma, and the polynomial-pair lemma in their source-shaped
   281	statements, with no divisibility hypothesis.  Their proofs retain the source
   282	constructions and mark the unresolved obligation at the exact steps: the
   283	first sampling step of the sub-line construction, where $\chi_{2m+2}$ and
   284	the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$ are invoked, and the
   285	instantiation step of the polynomial-pair proof, where $(q,2m+2,d,1)$ is
   286	used as a game parameter tuple.  A chapter remark records the divisibility
   287	arithmetic and cites this note; the final soundness theorem for the Pauli
   288	basis test remains open modulo this obligation.  An earlier revision had
   289	instead added the hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$ to the three lemmas; that was
   290	statement drift in the sense of the proof-gap protocol, since the hypothesis
   291	excludes all admissible $m \ge 2$ and does not appear in the source.
   292	
   293	\section{Conclusion}
   294	
   295	There is a theorem-level gap in the source proof route: the classical low
   296	individual degree game invoked at dimension $2m+2$ is undefined for every
   297	admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ (and for $(q,m) = (2,1)$), because its
   298	question distribution requires $2m+2 \mid q$ while admissibility supplies
   299	only $m \mid q$.  The cited route therefore does not establish the
   300	polynomial-pair lemma, nor the soundness of the Pauli basis test that
   301	depends on it, beyond $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.  We do not assert that the
   302	conclusion is false: the underlying tensor-code soundness is insensitive to
   303	how the axis index is sampled.  The recommended stage-4 route is the direct
   304	index sampling repair --- restate the imported soundness theorem for the
   305	directly indexed game at arbitrary dimension; prove that when the dimension
   306	divides $q$ the parsing map carries the conditionally linear question
   307	distribution onto the direct one; transport strategies between the two
   308	games, by parsing pullback in one direction and by seed-fiber averaging
   309	with a dilation--compression round trip in the other, so that the present
   310	soundness statement follows from the repaired import; and reread the
   311	combining subtree against the directly indexed game --- with dimension
   312	padding as the fallback confined to the present game definition.

    44	\section{Key theorem forms}
    45	
    46	Three statements must be kept apart.  Throughout, $\game$ denotes a symmetric
    47	two-player one-round game and $\eps \ge 0$ a real parameter; the notation is
    48	introduced in the next section.
    49	
    50	\begin{enumerate}
    51	  \item \textbf{Source form (attainment form).}  If
    52	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and projective
    53	  strategy $\strategy$ with $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps$.
    54	  \item \textbf{Approximate form (what the source proof establishes).}  If
    55	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then for every $\eps' > \eps$ there exists a
    56	  symmetric and projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    57	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps'$.
    58	  \item \textbf{Given-strategy form (value-preserving symmetrization).}  If
    59	  $\strategy'$ is any strategy for $\game$ with
    60	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and
    61	  projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    62	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$.
    63	\end{enumerate}
    64	
    65	The source proof consists exactly of a proof of the third form, applied to a
    66	strategy supplied by the definition of the supremum; this yields the second
    67	form.  The first form asserts strictly more than the second, and the passage
    68	from the second to the first is the gap discussed in this note.  Every use of
    69	the lemma, in the source and in this project, consumes only the second or the
    70	third form.
    71	
    72	\section{The source assertion}
    73	
    74	A two-player one-round game
    75	$\game = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ in compact symmetric notation
    76	consists of a finite question alphabet $\mathcal X$, a finite answer alphabet
    77	$\mathcal A$, a symmetric question distribution $\mu$ on
    78	$\mathcal X \times \mathcal X$, and a decision predicate $D$ treating the two
    79	players symmetrically.  A tensor product strategy
    80	$\strategy = (\ket\psi, A, B)$ consists of a unit vector $\ket\psi$ in a
    81	tensor product $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ of \emph{finite-dimensional}
    82	Hilbert spaces together with POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ for the two
    83	players; its value $\val^*(\game, \strategy)$ is the acceptance probability,
    84	and the value of the game is the supremum
    85	\begin{equation*}
    86	  \val^*(\game) = \sup_{\strategy} \val^*(\game, \strategy)
    87	\end{equation*}
    88	over all tensor product strategies.  A strategy is projective if all its
    89	measurements are projective, and symmetric if the state is
    90	permutation-invariant on $\mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$ and both players use the
    91	same measurements.
    92	
    93	The symmetrization lemma of \cite[Section~5]{Ji2020MIPStar} asserts:%
    94	\footnote{The statement is at
    95	\path{references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex}, lines~94--99,
    96	and its proof at lines~101--132.  The blueprint statement restored to this form
    97	is \path{lem:symmetric-strat} in
    98	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex}.}
    99	if $\game$ is a symmetric game with $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some
   100	$\eps \ge 0$, then
   101	\begin{equation*}
   102	  \exists\, \strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M) \text{ symmetric and projective}
   103	  \quad\text{with}\quad
   104	  \val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps.
   105	  \tag{\path{lem:symmetric-strat}}
   106	\end{equation*}
   107	
   108	Its proof runs as follows.  For every $\eps' > \eps$ the definition of the
   109	supremum supplies a strategy $\strategy' = (\ket{\psi'}, A, B)$ with
   110	$\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps'$.  By Naimark dilation in the completed
   111	projective form of \cite[Theorem~5.1]{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} one may take
   112	$\ket{\psi'} \in \C^d_{A'} \ot \C^d_{B'}$ for some integer $d$ with all
   113	measurements projective.  One then forms the permutation-invariant state
   114	\begin{equation*}
   115	  \ket{\psi} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}
   116	  \bigl( \ket{0}_A \ket{1}_B \ket{\psi'}_{A'B'}
   117	       + \ket{1}_A \ket{0}_B \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{A'B'} \bigr)
   118	\end{equation*}
   119	on $(\C^2 \ot \C^d) \ot (\C^2 \ot \C^d)$, where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ permutes
   120	the two players' registers, and the block-diagonal projective measurements
   121	$M^x_a = \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \ot A^x_a + \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \ot B^x_a$.  Symmetry
   122	of $D$ gives $\val^*(\game, (\ket\psi, M)) = \val^*(\game, \strategy')$.  The
   123	construction is therefore \emph{value-preserving}: applied to any strategy it
   124	produces a symmetric projective strategy of exactly the same value.  What the
   125	proof establishes is thus the given-strategy form, hence the approximate form;
   126	the printed conclusion is the attainment form.
   127	
   128	\section{Why attainment does not follow}
   129	
   130	The supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ ranges over strategies on
   131	finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces of unbounded dimension.  The strategies
   132	$\strategy'_{\eps'}$ produced for $\eps' \downarrow \eps$ may require
   133	dimensions $d(\eps')$ growing without bound, and there is no compactness
   134	across dimensions from which a limiting finite-dimensional strategy of value
   135	at least $1-\eps$ could be extracted.  A symmetric projective strategy of
   136	value at least $1-\eps = \val^*(\game)$ would attain the supremum, so the
   137	printed conclusion is equivalent, under its hypothesis, to the assertion that
   138	$\val^*(\game)$ is attained by some strategy.  No general principle supplies
   139	this: it is known, and recalled in the introduction of the source itself, that
   140	the set of finite-dimensional quantum correlations is not closed and differs
   141	from the set of infinite-dimensional spatial correlations, so limits of
   142	finite-dimensional strategies need not be realized by any finite-dimensional
   143	strategy.  Whether some symmetric game realizes the failure --- a game whose
   144	value is attained by no tensor product strategy, presented together with the
   145	exposing functional as a decision predicate --- is a separate question that
   146	this note does not need to settle.  The local verdict is about the proof: the
   147	cited argument proves the approximate form and does not prove the attainment
   148	form.
   149	
   150	\section{Uses of the lemma}
   151	
   152	The source invokes the lemma twice.
   153	
   154	First, in the soundness proof for the oracularization transformation, the
   155	argument fixes a strategy $\strategy^{\mathrm{orac}}$ for the oracularized game
   156	``with value $1-\eps$'' and applies the lemma to assume without loss of
   157	generality that it is projective.%
   158	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/10_oracularization.tex},
   159	lines~317--321.}
   160	Here the input is a given strategy, not the value of the game; the
   161	given-strategy form applies verbatim and preserves the value exactly, so the
   162	use is justified by what the proof establishes.
   163	
   164	Second, in the soundness proof for answer reduction, the argument assumes the
   165	strict inequality $\val^*(\game) > 1-\eps$ and concludes that there is a
   166	symmetric projective strategy of value greater than $1-\eps$.%
   167	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/11_answer_reduction.tex},
   168	lines~2322--2332.}
   169	Writing $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps_0$ with $\eps_0 < \eps$ and applying the
   170	approximate form with $\eps' = (\eps+\eps_0)/2$ produces a symmetric
   171	projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps' > 1-\eps$.  A strict lower
   172	bound on the supremum thus passes through the approximate form; attainment is
   173	not used.
   174	
   175	In this project, the soundness statements of the Pauli basis test track
   176	quantify over strategies assumed to succeed with probability at least
   177	$1-\eps$, so any symmetrization step starts from a given strategy and consumes
   178	the given-strategy form.  The blueprint currently records the lemma as part of
   179	the games vocabulary and has no downstream dependency on it; the two source
   180	uses above belong to transformations outside the scope of the present
   181	development.  Consequently, no consumer of the lemma --- in the source or here
   182	--- requires the attainment form.
   183	
   184	\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
   185	
   186	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} states the lemma in the source shape.
   187	Its proof records the value-preserving construction and the approximate form
   188	that the construction yields, and explicitly marks the remaining attainment
   189	step as unproved, citing this note; an accompanying remark summarizes the
   190	obstruction.  An earlier revision of the blueprint had instead weakened the
   191	source-labelled conclusion to the approximate form; following the project's
   192	proof-gap protocol, the source-labelled statement is restored and the missing
   193	step is tracked in the proof rather than absorbed into the statement.  No
   194	\Lean{} declaration is currently linked to the lemma.
   195	
   196	\section{Conclusion}
   197	
   198	The verdict is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma: the symmetrization
   199	argument proves the given-strategy and approximate forms, while the printed
   200	conclusion additionally asserts that the supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ is
   201	attained, which does not follow.  The gap is harmless for the results built on
   202	the lemma, since both uses in the source, and all planned uses in this
   203	project, proceed from a given strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ or from a
   204	strict lower bound on the value, for which the value-preserving construction
   205	suffices.  For stage~4 (formalization) the recommendation is: formalize the
   206	given-strategy symmetrization lemma as the workhorse statement; keep the
   207	source-labelled lemma in source shape with the attainment step an explicit,
   208	tracked proof obligation; and do not strengthen the source-labelled statement's
   209	hypotheses or weaken its conclusion silently.  If a later investigation
   210	settles the counterexample question for symmetric games, the statement should
   211	then be reclassified from an unproved step to a documented statement
   212	correction.

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197

   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}

     return [
         (m.group("title").strip(), m.group("star") is not None)
         for m in SECTION_RE.finditer(text)
     ]
 
 
 def _first_section_body(text: str) -> str:
     """Return the body of the first section, or the empty string if absent."""
 
     matches = list(SECTION_RE.finditer(text))
     if not matches:
         return ""
     start = matches[0].end()
     end = matches[1].start() if len(matches) > 1 else len(text)
     return text[start:end]
 
 
 def _scan_note_text(rel_path: str, text: str) -> list[Finding]:
     """Return style findings for one paper-gap note."""
 
     findings: list[Finding] = []
 
     def add(message: str) -> None:
         findings.append(Finding(rel_path, message))
 
     if "\\documentclass" not in text:
         add("missing LaTeX document class")
     if not XURL_RE.search(text):
         add("missing `\\usepackage{xurl}`")
     if not COMMAND_INPUT_RE.search(text):
         add("missing shared paper-gap macros: `\\input{command}`")
     if "\\begin{document}" not in text or "\\end{document}" not in text:
         add("missing document body delimiters")
 
     sections = _section_titles(text)
     if len(sections) < 2:
         add("missing first two sections `At a glance` and `Key theorem forms`")
     else:
         first_title, first_starred = sections[0]
         second_title, second_starred = sections[1]
         if first_starred or first_title != "At a glance":
             add("Section 1 must be an unstarred `At a glance` section")
         if second_starred or not second_title.startswith("Key theorem forms"):
             add("Section 2 must be an unstarred `Key theorem forms` section")
 
     first_body = _first_section_body(text).lower()
     if first_body:
         if "difficulty" not in first_body:
             add("the `At a glance` section should state the difficulty")
         if "estimated weight" not in first_body:
             add("the `At a glance` section should state the estimated weight")
         if "mathlib/project split" not in first_body:
             add("the `At a glance` section should state the Mathlib/project split")
         has_key_inputs = (
             "key mathlib inputs" in first_body
             or "key mathematical inputs" in first_body
         )
         if not has_key_inputs:
             add(
                 "the `At a glance` section should state the key Mathlib or "
                 "mathematical inputs"
             )
 
     if "\\section{Conclusion}" not in text:
         add("missing `Conclusion` section")
     if "\\bibliographystyle{alpha}" not in text:
         add("missing `\\bibliographystyle{alpha}`")
     if "\\bibliography{references}" not in text:
         add("missing `\\bibliography{references}`")
     if not CITE_RE.search(text):
         add("missing bibliographic citation such as `\\cite{...}`")
-    if "\\ghissue{" not in text and "\\ghpr{" not in text:
-        add("missing GitHub traceability macro `\\ghissue{...}` or `\\ghpr{...}`")
+    if ("\\ghissue{" not in text and "\\ghpr{" not in text
+            and "\\localissue{" not in text):
+        add("missing traceability macro `\\ghissue{...}`, `\\ghpr{...}`, "
+            "or `\\localissue{...}`")
 
     if TEXTTT_TRACE_RE.search(text):
         add("use paper-gap macros instead of `\\texttt{...}` for Lean or source traceability")
     if RAW_LEAN_ID_RE.search(text):
         add("wrap fully qualified Lean names with `\\leanid{...}`")
     if RAW_PAPER_PATH_RE.search(text):
         add("wrap paper source paths with `\\path{...}`")
 
     return findings
 
 
 def scan_changed_notes(root: Path, changed_files: list[str]) -> list[Finding]:
     """Return findings for changed paper-gap notes."""
 
     findings: list[Finding] = []
     for rel_path in sorted({path for path in changed_files if _is_note_file(path)}):
         path = root / rel_path
         if not path.exists():
             continue
         text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
         findings.extend(_scan_note_text(rel_path, text))
     return findings
 
 
 def _parse_args(argv: list[str]) -> argparse.Namespace:
     parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
     parser.add_argument("--root", type=Path, default=Path("."))
     parser.add_argument("--base", default="origin/main")
     parser.add_argument("--staged", action="store_true")
     parser.add_argument("--changed-files", nargs="*")
     parser.add_argument("--changed-files-file", type=Path)
     parser.add_argument("--ci", action="store_true")
     return parser.parse_args(argv)
 
 
 def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
     args = _parse_args(sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv)
     root = args.root.resolve()
 
     try:
         if args.changed_files_file is not None:
             changed_files = _read_changed_files_file(args.changed_files_file)
         elif args.changed_files is not None:
             changed_files = list(args.changed_files)
         else:
             changed_files = _changed_files_from_git(root, base=args.base, staged=args.staged)
     except RuntimeError as exc:
         print(f"check_paper_gap_note_style.py: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
         return 2
 
     findings = scan_changed_notes(root, changed_files)
     if findings:
         print("Paper-gap note style findings:", file=sys.stderr)
         for finding in findings:
             print(f"  {finding.file}: {finding.message}", file=sys.stderr)
         return 1 if args.ci else 0
 
     if args.ci:
         checked = sum(1 for path in changed_files if _is_note_file(path))
         print(f"Paper-gap note style check passed for {checked} changed note(s).")
     return 0
 
 
 if __name__ == "__main__":
     raise SystemExit(main())

1	\chapter{Games, strategies, and conditionally linear distributions}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-games}
     3	% Paper label sec:games kept for cross-reference fidelity; resolves to the chapter number.
     4	\label{sec:games}
     5	
     6	This chapter records the vocabulary in which the quantum Pauli basis test and its analysis are phrased: two-player one-round games and tensor product strategies, the consistency and state-dependent distance calculus for families of measurements, and conditionally linear functions and distributions, the class of question distributions used by the tests of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. The presentation follows \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}; the distance calculus is imported there from \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP} and \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.
     7	
     8	\section{Measurements and observables}
     9	
    10	\begin{definition}[POVMs, sub-measurements, and observables]\label{def:povm-conventions}
    11		\uses{def:submeasurement}
    12		% Finiteness of the outcome set is stated explicitly here; the source leaves it implicit,
    13		% and the measurement and submeasurement definitions referenced below assume finite

    15		Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued measures (POVMs).    229	\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}

   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.

   242	  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new

30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]

    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.

    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}

   145	follows.

   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a

   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a

   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
